after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
The second-order differential equation ${y}^{″}-2{y}^{′}+y=0$
can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where 

$$
x(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}],\,y(t)={x}_{1}(t),\,{y}^{′}(t)={x}_{2}(t).
$$

Find the matrix $A.$
after.worked_solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=2{y}^{′}-y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=2{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=-{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Hence, $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].$

x(t)=[x1x2],A=[abcd],y(t)=x1(t),y′(t)=x2(t). Find the matrix A.

We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

{x1′=x2,x2′=y″.

content.knowledge_point: Writing a Homogeneous ODE as a Matrix Differential Equation
content.problem:
The second-order differential equation ${y}^{″}-2{y}^{′}+y=0$
can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where 

$$
x(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}],\,y(t)={x}_{1}(t),\,{y}^{′}(t)={x}_{2}(t).
$$

Find the matrix $A.$
content.worked_solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=2{y}^{′}-y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=2{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=-{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Hence, $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].$

$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(1)=3 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=16{x}_{1}+8{x}_{2},\, & {x}_{2}(1)=1\end{aligned}

decision.explanation: The initial conditions give p=−1 and q=2, so p−q=−3. The equation gives f(t)=y″=10x₂−25sin(t)x₁. Thus (p−q)f(t)=75sin(t)x₁−30x₂=15(5sin(t)x₁−2x₂), matching option d.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
The second-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-10{y}^{′}+25\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,y=0,\,y(0)=-1,\,{y}^{′}(0)=2
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(0)=p \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=f(t),\, & {x}_{2}(0)=q\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t),$ and $p$ and $q$ are constants. Calculate  $(p-q)\cdot f(t).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′}.\end{aligned}
$$

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & ={x}_{1}(0)=-1 \\ {y}^{′}(0) & ={x}_{2}(0)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=10{y}^{′}-25\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=10{x}_{2}-25\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(0)=-1 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=-25\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{1}+10{x}_{2},\, & {x}_{2}(0)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $p=-1,q=2,f(t)=-25\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{1}+10{x}_{2},$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}(p-q)\cdot f(t) & =(-1-2)(-25\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{1}+10{x}_{2}) \\  & =-3(-5)(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}) \\  & =15(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Reducing a Homogeneous Initial Value Problem to a First-Order System
content.problem:
The second-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-10{y}^{′}+25\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,y=0,\,y(0)=-1,\,{y}^{′}(0)=2
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(0)=p \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=f(t),\, & {x}_{2}(0)=q\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t),$ and $p$ and $q$ are constants. Calculate  $(p-q)\cdot f(t).$
content.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′}.\end{aligned}
$$

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & ={x}_{1}(0)=-1 \\ {y}^{′}(0) & ={x}_{2}(0)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=10{y}^{′}-25\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=10{x}_{2}-25\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(0)=-1 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=-25\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{1}+10{x}_{2},\, & {x}_{2}(0)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $p=-1,q=2,f(t)=-25\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{1}+10{x}_{2},$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}(p-q)\cdot f(t) & =(-1-2)(-25\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{1}+10{x}_{2}) \\  & =-3(-5)(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}) \\  & =15(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
The third-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{‴}+{y}^{″}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,y=0,\,y(0)=2,\,{y}^{′}(0)=-1,\,{y}^{″}(0)=4
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(0)=p \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3},\, & {x}_{2}(0)=q \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=f(t),\, & {x}_{3}(0)=r\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t),$ ${x}_{3}(t)={y}^{″}(t),$ and $p,$ $q$ and $r$ are constants. Calculate  $(p-q-r)\cdot f(t).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & ={x}_{1}(0)=2 \\ {y}^{′}(0) & ={x}_{2}(0)=-1 \\ {y}^{″}(0) & ={x}_{3}(0)=4\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}=-{y}^{″}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}=-{x}_{3}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(0)=2 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3},\, & {x}_{2}(0)=-1 \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{3},\, & {x}_{3}(0)=4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $p=2,q=-1,r=4,f(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{3},$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}(p-q-r)\cdot f(t) & =(2-(-1)-4)(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{3}) \\  & =(2+1-4)(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{3}) \\  & =(-1)(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{3}) \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

y(0)=x1(0)=2y′(0)=x2(0)=−1y″(0)=x3(0)=4

Differentiating the above equations with respect to t, we get x1′(t)=y′x2′(t)=y″x3′(t)=y‴

which we can rewrite as

{x1′=x2,x2′=x3,x3′=y‴.

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of x1,x2, and x3.

Finally, p=2,q=−1,r=4,f(t)=2cos⁡tx1−x3, and

(p−q−r)⋅f(t)=(2−(−1)−4)(2cos⁡tx1−x3)=(2+1−4)(2cos⁡tx1−x3)=(−1)(2cos⁡tx1−x3)=−2cos⁡tx1+x3.

content.knowledge_point: Reducing a Homogeneous Initial Value Problem to a First-Order System
content.problem:
The third-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{‴}+{y}^{″}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,y=0,\,y(0)=2,\,{y}^{′}(0)=-1,\,{y}^{″}(0)=4
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(0)=p \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3},\, & {x}_{2}(0)=q \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=f(t),\, & {x}_{3}(0)=r\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t),$ ${x}_{3}(t)={y}^{″}(t),$ and $p,$ $q$ and $r$ are constants. Calculate  $(p-q-r)\cdot f(t).$
content.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

We also convert the initial conditions, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & ={x}_{1}(0)=2 \\ {y}^{′}(0) & ={x}_{2}(0)=-1 \\ {y}^{″}(0) & ={x}_{3}(0)=4\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}=-{y}^{″}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}=-{x}_{3}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2},\, & {x}_{1}(0)=2 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3},\, & {x}_{2}(0)=-1 \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{3},\, & {x}_{3}(0)=4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $p=2,q=-1,r=4,f(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{3},$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}(p-q-r)\cdot f(t) & =(2-(-1)-4)(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{3}) \\  & =(2+1-4)(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{3}) \\  & =(-1)(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{x}_{1}-{x}_{3}) \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
The second-order differential equation ${y}^{″}-4{t}^{3}{y}^{′}-5ty=0$
can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where 

$$
x(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}],\,y(t)={x}_{1}(t),\,{y}^{′}(t)={x}_{2}(t).
$$

Find the matrix $A.$
after.worked_solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=4{t}^{3}{y}^{′}+5ty.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=4{t}^{3}{x}_{2}+5t{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=5t{x}_{1}+4{t}^{3}{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 5t & 4{t}^{3}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Hence, $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 5t & 4{t}^{3}\end{aligned}].$

content.problem:
The second-order differential equation ${y}^{″}-4{t}^{3}{y}^{′}-5ty=0$
can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where 

$$
x(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}],\,y(t)={x}_{1}(t),\,{y}^{′}(t)={x}_{2}(t).
$$

Find the matrix $A.$
content.worked_solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=4{t}^{3}{y}^{′}+5ty.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=4{t}^{3}{x}_{2}+5t{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=5t{x}_{1}+4{t}^{3}{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 5t & 4{t}^{3}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Hence, $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 5t & 4{t}^{3}\end{aligned}].$
